docs.title: RedGem 3D Engine
docs.text:
RedGem is a 3D game engine with its own editor. You build levels in the editor (or in Blender), write the gameplay in Ruby, press Play, and export a standalone game.

This manual is for people making games with it.

docs.title: Where to start
docs.text:
1. Install the editor.
  2. Follow Your first game: about fifteen minutes from an empty folder to a playable game.
  3. Keep Behaviours and the API reference open while you write scripts.

docs.title: How a game is organized
docs.text:
A game is a folder:

Path What it is scene.glb The main level: objects, meshes, lights, cameras scenes/*.glb More levels scripts/*.rb Ruby behaviours and scene scripts models/*.glb Models you can drop into a level sounds/ .wav, .ogg, .mp3 or .flac files game.json Window title and size

The editor reads and writes these files directly. There is no project database and no import step: what you see in the folder is the game.

docs.title: Working on the engine
docs.text: For people changing RedGem itself. To make games with it, the rest of this manual is enough.

docs.title: Demos
docs.text:
Demos: games/city (a crossroad with Ruby-driven traffic: lights, braking, spinning wheels; Kenney CC0 models), games/platformer (WASD/arrows, Space jumps: grab 5 coins, reach the flag) and games/driving (W/S throttle, A/D steer, Space hand brake, R reset: drive laps).

Showcase (games/showcase, not committed: it is built from downloaded assets). A street at dusk with a drivable car, traffic that keeps its distance and overtakes, parked cars, shop fronts and cafe tables, a crowd on the sidewalks, potholes and falling leaves, made to push the renderer. Blender only builds the scene; everything that happens in it is set up in games/showcase/scripts/main_scene.rb:

python3 -I tools/assets/fetch_showcase.py      # street: Poly Haven and ambientCG (CC0)
python3 -I tools/assets/fetch_ad_assets.py     # car and people: BlenderKit (see showcase/CREDITS.md)
SHOWCASE_RENDER=0 BLENDER_MEMORY_MAX=8500M tools/blender/run.sh build_showcase.py showcase
./build/src/redgem games/showcase           # then Play: WASD drives, Space brakes

The export needs about 7 GB of memory (close the editor first); without SHOWCASE_RENDER=0 it also renders showcase/renders/ad.png with Cycles, which needs an NVIDIA RTX card. games/city is rebuilt with tools/assets/fetch_kenney.sh and tools/blender/run.sh build_city.py games/city.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
cd build && ctest --output-on-failure        # everything
ctest -L system                              # only the system tests

A system test is a Ruby file run against a game: redgem <game_dir> --test <file.rb> [--screenshots <dir>] [--headless] (--headless runs without a window; redgem --help lists every option).

  • C++ unit + integration (doctest): math, extras parser, glTF loading from Blender fixtures, scene hierarchy, physics world, Ruby VM, and a headless engine running the sandbox fixture game.
  • Ruby tests run inside the engine's mruby: redgem --ruby-test tests/ruby/vector3_test.rb.
  • Editor system test (tests/editor_system/) opens the editor window on a copy of the platformer, picks, edits, plays, stops, undoes and saves.
  • System tests (tests/system/<game>/*_test.rb, run against games/<game>) open the real game window and drive it frame by frame with simulated input:
SystemTest.define do |t|
  t.hold(:w, frames: 60)
  t.wait_until(frames: 30) { Scene.find("Coin1").nil? }
  t.assert("score counts the coin") { GameManager.instance.coins == 1 }
  t.screenshot("collect_coin_after")        # saved to build/screenshots/<game>/
end

Test fixtures are regenerated with tools/blender/run.sh build_test_fixtures.py tests/fixtures.

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
src/core      constants (config.hpp), math, logging, fixed timestep clock
src/scene     glTF loader (meshes, skeletons, animations), Blender extras parser, scene graph,
              animation playback
src/physics   PhysicsWorld interface + Jolt implementation
src/input     keys, axes/actions, keyboard and scripted input sources
src/audio     sound effects and music (raylib, or a recorder for tests)
src/script    mruby VM, behaviour host, native bindings
src/render    renderer (HDR, shadows, reflections, post-processing), shaders, environment,
              culling, graphics card choice, mesh conversion
src/editor    editor: scene document (undo, save, import), session (play mode), camera, picking,
              project hub, script tabs, ImGui panels and theme (src/editor/ui)
src/app       engine loop, game projects (templates, build, recent games), user settings and
              command line
ruby/engine   Ruby prelude embedded in the binary (Behaviour, Vector3, test DSLs)
templates     scripts of the new-game templates (embedded in the binary)
assets/editor fonts of the editor (Inter, JetBrains Mono; SIL Open Font License, see the license files)
games         demo games: scene.glb, scripts and the .blend each scene was built from
showcase      renders of the showcase scene and the credits of its assets
tools/blender scene builders (run with tools/blender/run.sh), walk_rig.py
tools/assets  downloaders of the free assets the demos use
tests         unit, integration, Ruby and system tests, with their fixtures
cmake         dependencies (pinned versions) and file embedding

docs.title: Not there yet
docs.text:
• Choosing which animation plays: every animation in a scene loops at once (fine for one clip per character). Characters copied with Duplicate in the editor keep the pose they were copied in.
  • Spot light cones, and camera clip planes from the scene (the engine uses fixed ones).
  • Reusing data when the same model is imported twice, and dropping the data of deleted imports from scene.glb (each import appends its meshes and textures).
  • Mirrored objects (negative scale) are drawn inside out.
  • More vehicle options from Blender properties (drive layout, engine torque); hot reload of scripts while playing.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
./build/src/redgem games/platformer          # opens the editor
./build/src/redgem games/platformer --play   # just plays the game

The editor is built with Dear ImGui (dark theme, Inter and JetBrains Mono fonts, Font Awesome icons):

  • Toolbar: move / rotate / scale gizmos, local or world axes, grid snapping (or hold Ctrl while dragging), Play / Pause / Stop, and Build.
  • Hierarchy: the object tree with search. Click to select, double click to frame, drag onto another object to parent it (or onto empty space to unparent), right click for actions and to create objects. Scripts and models from the Project panel can be dropped on it.
  • Scene: hold the right mouse button and use WASD/QE to fly, wheel to dolly, F to frame the selection, click to pick objects, W / E / R switch the gizmo. Drop a model on the ground to place it there, or a script on an object to attach it.
  • Inspector: name, tag, visible, Template (hidden in the game, copied with Scene.spawn), then one card per component: Transform, Mesh with its materials (color, metallic, roughness, emission), Light (type, color, intensity, range), Camera (field of view, clipping), one card per Ruby script, Physics (body, trigger, collider, mass), vehicle wheels and custom properties. Add Component adds scripts (existing or new), a physics body, a trigger or a property.
  • GameObject menu: empty objects, cube / sphere / plane / cylinder / capsule (with colliders), directional / point / spot lights, cameras, and models from models/.
  • Project: the game's scripts, models, sounds and scenes. Double click a script to edit it, a model to add it to the scene, a sound to hear it. New script creates a Behaviour from a template; Open folder shows the files.
  • Console: engine and Ruby output (filter by level), including script errors with backtraces.
  • Scripts: each open Ruby file gets its own tab next to the Scene. Drag tabs to split the view anywhere (or press Split right), like a code editor's editor groups. Ctrl+S saves and checks the syntax (errors show the line); Open externally uses your default editor. Play saves all open scripts and reloads them.
  • View menu: hide the Hierarchy (Ctrl+B), the Inspector (Ctrl+Alt+B) or the bottom panels (Ctrl+J) to give the scene or the code more room; the toolbar's outer buttons toggle the sides.
  • Play / Pause / Stop (Ctrl+P, Esc): runs the game inside the Scene view with the current edits and fresh scripts; Stop restores the scene exactly as it was.
  • Ctrl+Z / Ctrl+Y undo and redo, Ctrl+D duplicate, Del delete, Ctrl+S save. Help > Keyboard Shortcuts lists them all. File > New / Open Game goes back to the hub.

Saving rewrites scene.glb in place (only the glTF JSON; meshes and textures are untouched), so the file still opens in Blender. When the file changes on disk (e.g. you re-export from Blender) the editor reloads it automatically, unless you have unsaved edits.

docs.title: Your first game
docs.text: You will create a game from a template, change it, write a behaviour in Ruby and export it.

docs.title: 1. Create the game
docs.text:
Start RedGem with no arguments. In the project hub, pick the Platformer template, type a name and create it. The same from a terminal:

./build/src/redgem new ~/RedGemGames/my_game --template platformer
./build/src/redgem ~/RedGemGames/my_game

With Docker, write tools/docker/editor.sh wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem.

The editor opens:

  • Scene (center): the level. Hold the right mouse button and use WASD to fly, scroll to move closer, click an object to select it.
  • Hierarchy (left): every object of the level.
  • Inspector (right): what the selected object is made of.
  • Project and Console (bottom): the game's files, and messages from the engine and from your scripts.

docs.title: 2. Play it
docs.text: Press Play in the toolbar (or Ctrl+P). The game runs inside the Scene view: WASD moves, Space jumps. Press Esc or Stop to go back to editing. The level returns exactly to how it was.

docs.title: 3. Change the level
docs.text:
1. Click a coin in the Scene view.
  2. Drag the arrows of the gizmo to move it somewhere harder to reach.
  3. Press Ctrl+D to duplicate it and move the copy too.
  4. Press Ctrl+S to save.

Ctrl+Z undoes any of this.

docs.title: 4. Write a behaviour
docs.text:
Make the hero's coins worth collecting: a platform that moves up and down.

  1. In the menu, GameObject > 3D Object > Cube. Scale and place it as a platform.
  2. In the Inspector, Add Component > Script, type bob and press New.
  3. The script opens in a tab next to the Scene. Replace its contents with:
# Moves the object up and down.
class Bob < Behaviour
  HEIGHT = 2.0   # meters
  SECONDS = 4.0  # per cycle

  def start
    @origin = transform.position
  end

  def update(_dt)
    wave = Math.sin(Time.elapsed / SECONDS * 2 * Math::PI)
    transform.position = @origin + Vector3.up * (wave * HEIGHT)
  end
end
  1. Press Ctrl+S. The tab shows Syntax OK, or the line of the mistake.
  2. With the cube selected, find the Physics card in the Inspector and set Body to kinematic, so the hero can stand on it while it moves.
  3. Press Play.

If a script fails while the game runs, the game keeps going: that behaviour is switched off and the error, with its line, appears in the Console.

docs.title: 5. Share it
docs.text: Build in the toolbar (or redgem build <game> <folder>) makes a folder with your game's executable and its files. Zip it and send it. See Building and sharing.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• Behaviours: how scripts are attached and what they can do.
  • Gameplay recipes: input, movement, pickups, HUD, sound, levels.

docs.title: Install
docs.text: RedGem runs on Linux. Pick one of the two ways below.

docs.title: With Docker (easiest)
docs.text:
You need Docker and a desktop session using X11.

git clone <repository URL> redgem
cd redgem
tools/docker/editor.sh

The first run builds the image, which takes a few minutes. After that the editor opens in seconds.

  • Games you create are saved in ~/RedGemGames on your machine.
  • The demos are in the games/ folder of the checkout: tools/docker/editor.sh games/platformer.
  • The script takes the same arguments as redgem itself, so wherever this manual says ./build/src/redgem ..., write tools/docker/editor.sh .... Paths must be inside ~/RedGemGames or the checkout's games/ folder: the container sees nothing else.
  • The container has no sound.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
You need a C++17 compiler, CMake 3.24 or newer, Ninja, Ruby with rake, and the X11 and OpenGL development files. On Ubuntu or Debian:

sudo apt install build-essential cmake ninja-build git ca-certificates xz-utils ruby rake bison \
  libgl1-mesa-dev libx11-dev libxrandr-dev libxinerama-dev libxcursor-dev libxi-dev libasound2-dev

Then:

cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja
cmake --build build
./build/src/redgem

CMake downloads the libraries RedGem is built on at fixed versions. The first build takes a few minutes.

docs.title: Check that it works
docs.text: ./build/src/redgem (or tools/docker/editor.sh) opens the project hub. Choose Platformer under New game, give it a name, and the editor opens with a level you can play right away: press the Play button, move with WASD, jump with Space.

docs.title: Blender (optional)
docs.text: You can make whole games without it. Install Blender 4.x when you want to model your own objects or build levels there: see Levels, lighting and Blender.

docs.title: How a scene is made
docs.text:
1. Model the level in Blender. Gameplay is configured with custom properties (Object Properties → Custom Properties), e.g. script = "coin.rb", trigger = true.
  2. Export to scene.glb (glTF binary). The exporter writes custom properties to each node's extras.
  3. The runtime loads the .glb with cgltf, reads the extras, builds physics bodies and instantiates the Ruby class named after each script (camera_follow.rb → CameraFollow).

A game is just a folder:

games/platformer/
  scene.glb          # exported from Blender
  platformer.blend   # the editable source
  scripts/*.rb       # behaviours

docs.title: Look of a scene: environment, lights and effects
docs.text:
Scenes are drawn in HDR and finished with bloom (bright things glow), filmic tone mapping, a vignette and anti-aliasing. One object with the property environment = true (GameObject > Environment in the editor, or a Blender empty) sets the mood through its properties:

Property Meaning sky_top, sky_horizon, ground_color colors of the sky gradient, as #rrggbb; they also light the scene fog_color, fog_density distance fog (it follows the horizon color unless given its own) ambient, exposure strength of the sky's light, overall brightness bloom, vignette, sun_glow glow around bright things, dark corners, the sun's disc and halo (0 turns each off) wind how much foliage sways shadows darkness of the sun's shadows (0 = none, 1 = full) ambient_occlusion darkening of creases and contact areas (0 = none, 1 = full)

Without one, scenes get a clear day. Other things worth knowing: the 16 point lights nearest to the camera are used each frame (so a street can have dozens of lamps); the sun casts soft shadows around the camera; materials use their glTF normal, roughness/metallic, occlusion and emission textures; and textured materials with transparency are cut out by their alpha and sway with the wind (leaves, fences).

Glossy surfaces reflect their surroundings: the engine keeps capturing the scene around the camera (one cube face per frame) and uses it for reflections and ambient light.

Animated characters. glTF skeletons and animations are supported: skinned meshes are deformed on the GPU (up to 64 bones per skeleton, 4 per vertex) and every animation in the scene plays in a loop. The editor keeps skeletons and animations when saving, reordering or importing models. tools/blender/walk_rig.py gives a scanned standing person leg bones and a walk cycle.

Per-object color. The property tint = "#rrggbb" multiplies the colors of an object's mesh, so copies sharing one mesh (cars, crates) can each have their own color.

Graphics card. On laptops with two cards the engine asks for the dedicated one and logs which card it got. To choose: Edit > Graphics Card in the editor (saved in ~/.config/redgem/settings.json, used from the next start), the REDGEM_GPU environment variable, or --gpu auto|dedicated|integrated for one run. The command line wins over the environment, which wins over the saved setting.

Performance. Objects outside the view, and parts too small to see from where the camera is, are not drawn. What costs most is the number of separate objects on screen, more than their triangles: join the parts of a model that share a material, and give heavy models lighter versions for far away with visible_from and visible_to.

docs.title: Editing the level in Blender
docs.text:
blender games/platformer/platformer.blend           # edit, save
blender -b games/platformer/platformer.blend \
  --python tools/blender/export_scene.py -- games/platformer/scene.glb

tools/blender/run.sh build_platformer.py games/platformer (or build_driving.py games/driving) regenerates a whole level from code; tools/blender/scene_kit.py has helpers to build levels with bpy.

docs.title: Custom properties
docs.text:
Property Values Meaning script "player.rb" or "a.rb, b.rb" Behaviours to attach, loaded from scripts/ body static, dynamic, kinematic, character, vehicle Physics body (characters use Jolt's CharacterVirtual, vehicles its VehicleConstraint) wheel true On a child of a vehicle: it becomes a wheel (model it with its axle along X) collider box, sphere, capsule, mesh Shape, sized from the mesh bounds × object scale. collider alone = static body trigger true Trigger volume: fires on_trigger_enter/exit, does not collide mass number Mass of dynamic bodies tag string Used by Scene.find_all(tag) and game_object.tag? visible false Hide the mesh (the object still exists) prefab true A template: hidden and inert in the game, copied by Scene.spawn visible_from, visible_to meters The object is drawn only while that far from the camera: give a model a detailed version up close and a light one far away tint "#rrggbb" Multiplies the colors of this object's mesh (copies sharing a mesh can differ) environment true This object's properties set the sky, fog and effects (see "Look of a scene") anything number / string / bool Available in Ruby as props[:name] / prop(:name, default)

Cameras and lights (sun, point) are taken from the Blender scene. Spot lights are loaded but lit like point lights (in every direction). Parenting is preserved.

Vehicles. Give the chassis body = "vehicle" and parent the wheel meshes to it with wheel = true. Wheels in front of the center (Blender +Y) steer, the rear ones get the hand brake, and every axle is driven. Wheel radius and width come from the wheel mesh. See tools/blender/build_driving.py. Blender is Z-up; the engine is Y-up like glTF: Blender (x, y, z) is engine (x, z, -y) (Vector3.blender(x, y, z) does the conversion). Forward is -Z (Blender +Y).

docs.title: Building and sharing
docs.text:
Build in the editor's toolbar, or from a terminal:

./build/src/redgem build my_game dist/my_game

This makes a folder with an executable named after your game (dist/my_game/my_game) and a game/ folder with its files. Whoever receives the folder runs the executable: they do not need RedGem, Ruby or Blender installed.

  • The executable runs on Linux, like the engine. It needs the game/ folder next to it.
  • game.json sets the window title and size:
{ "title": "My Game", "window_width": 1280, "window_height": 720 }
  • Everything in the game folder is copied, including the scripts as plain .rb files.
  • Check the licenses of the models and sounds you include. A license that allows using an asset in a game does not always allow shipping its original file.

docs.title: Testing your game
docs.text:
The example below tests the game made in Your first game.

A system test is a Ruby script that plays your game: it holds keys, waits, checks what happened and can take screenshots. It runs the real game, frame by frame, at the same pace on any machine.

# tests/collect_coin_test.rb
SystemTest.define do |t|
  t.wait(30)                                   # frames
  t.hold(:w, frames: 60)                       # walk forward for a second
  t.wait_until(frames: 30) { Scene.find("Coin1").nil? }
  t.assert("the score counts the coin") { Scene.find("Player").get_component(Player).coins == 1 }
  t.screenshot("coin_collected")
end

Run it:

./build/src/redgem my_game --test tests/collect_coin_test.rb --screenshots shots

The command exits with an error when an assertion fails or a script raises, so it fits in any automated check. Add --headless to run without opening a window (no screenshots then).

docs.title: What a test can do
docs.text:
Call Effect t.wait(frames) Lets the game run t.hold(:w, :a, frames: 60) Holds keys for that long t.press(:space) Taps a key t.hold_until(:w, frames: 300) { ... } Holds keys until the block is true t.wait_until(frames: 120) { ... } Waits until the block is true, or fails t.assert("message") { ... } Fails the test when the block is false t.screenshot("name") Saves name.png in the screenshots folder

Inside the blocks you have the whole scripting API, so a test can also move objects or read any behaviour's state.

docs.title: What RedGem does not do yet
docs.text:
Knowing this up front saves time:

  • Input is keyboard only. There is no mouse or gamepad input for games.
  • In-game interface is text (UI.text). There are no buttons, images or menus.
  • Saving progress has no API.
  • Particles do not exist; small effects are objects moved by a script.
  • Animation: every animation in a level loops all the time. You cannot pick which one plays.
  • Platforms: Linux.
  • Scripts are loaded when you press Play; they are not reloaded while the game runs.

docs.title: Common problems
docs.text:
The editor does not open from Docker. Your session must use X11 (echo $XDG_SESSION_TYPE prints x11). The launcher tools/docker/editor.sh allows the container on your display and removes that permission when the editor closes.

The build fails looking for X11 headers. Install the development packages listed in Install. If you cannot install packages, tools/setup/fetch_x11_headers.sh extracts the headers into the project.

My script does nothing. Look at the Console: a script with an error is switched off and reported there. Check that the class name matches the file name (moving_door.rb defines MovingDoor) and that it inherits from Behaviour.

on_trigger_enter never fires. The object needs Trigger on, and the thing entering must be a character, a dynamic body or a kinematic body. Static scenery does not set triggers off.

The hero falls through a platform I move from a script. Give the platform a kinematic body. A static body is not meant to move.

The game is slow on a laptop with two graphics cards. RedGem asks for the dedicated card and logs which one it got when it starts. To choose: Edit > Graphics Card in the editor, or start with --gpu dedicated.

I changed the level in Blender and the editor did not update. It reloads scene.glb by itself when you have no unsaved edits. With unsaved edits it asks.

docs.title: API reference
docs.text:
The classes and methods scripts use most. For how they fit together, see Behaviours and Gameplay recipes.

Object Highlights Behaviour start, update(dt), fixed_update(dt), on_trigger_enter/exit(other), on_collision_enter/exit(other), on_destroy; helpers game_object, name, transform, character, rigidbody, vehicle, props, prop, find, find_all, destroy, get_component GameObject name, tag, tag?, props, alive?, destroy, visible / visible=, behaviours, parent, children, transform, character, rigidbody, vehicle, get_component(Klass), add_component(Klass, speed: 2.0), animation_offset(=) (seconds a spawned copy's animations run ahead of the original's) Transform position(=), local_position(=), rotation(=) (Euler degrees), rotate, look_at, translate, scale(=), forward, right, up CharacterController move(velocity), jump(speed), grounded?, velocity Rigidbody velocity(=), add_impulse(vector) Vehicle drive(throttle:, steering:, brake:, handbrake:), stop, speed (m/s, signed), velocity Physics raycast(origin, direction, max_distance = 1000, ignore = nil) → {object:, point:, normal:, distance:} or nil Input axis(:horizontal / :vertical), down?(:space), pressed?, released?, action?(:jump), action_pressed? Time delta, fixed_delta, elapsed, frame Scene / Camera Scene.find(name), Scene.find_all(tag), Scene.objects, Camera.main SceneScript setup, find, find_all, find! (see Setting a level up in Ruby) Scene.spawn Scene.spawn("Bullet", position: v, rotation: euler) copies a prefab = true template (hidden and inert in the game) with its physics and scripts; copies of animated characters move like the original Audio Audio.play(:jump, volume:, pitch:), Audio.music(:theme, loop: true, volume: 0.7), Audio.stop_music, Audio.volume = 0.8 (files in sounds/) UI / Debug / Game UI.text(str, x:, y:, size:, color:, alpha:), Debug.log/warn/error, Game.quit, Game.screenshot(name), Game.load_scene("level2") (scenes/level2.glb; "main" is scene.glb; Ruby globals survive), Game.scene_name Vector3 Vector3.new(x, y, z), Vector3.zero, one, up, down, left, right, forward, back; arithmetic, dot, cross, length, normalized, lerp, flat, with(y: 0), distance_to, approx?, to_a

Script errors are logged with a backtrace and only disable the failing behaviour; the game keeps running. Assigning transform.position to a physics object teleports it (moving bodies also stop); changing its rotation keeps its velocity. Vehicle wheel meshes must have their rotation applied (axle along X).

docs.title: Behaviours
docs.text:
A behaviour is a Ruby class that inherits from Behaviour. Attached to an object, it gets one instance for that object, and the engine calls its methods as the game runs.

class Door < Behaviour
  def start; end                      # once, before the first update
  def update(dt); end                 # every frame; dt is seconds since the last one
  def fixed_update(dt); end           # 60 times per second, with the physics
  def on_trigger_enter(other); end    # something entered this object's trigger (or it entered one)
  def on_trigger_exit(other); end
  def on_collision_enter(other); end  # this object's body touched another
  def on_collision_exit(other); end
  def on_destroy; end
end

Define only the ones you need. other is the other object (a GameObject).

docs.title: Files and class names
docs.text:
The file name decides the class name: camera_follow.rb must define CameraFollow. Scripts live in the game's scripts/ folder.

You never require another script. The first time you use a class name, RedGem loads the file it should be in (Patrol loads scripts/patrol.rb). That works for plain helper classes too.

docs.title: Attaching a behaviour
docs.text:
There are three ways, and they mix freely:

  • In the editor: Inspector > Add Component, or drag a script from the Project panel onto an object.
  • In Blender: the custom property script = "door.rb" (several: "door.rb, sound.rb").
  • From Ruby: object.add_component(Door, speed: 2.0).

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
A behaviour reads its settings with prop:

def start
  @speed = prop(:speed, 3.0)   # 3.0 when nothing sets it
end

prop(:speed, default) returns, in this order: what add_component was given, the object's custom property speed (set in the Inspector or in Blender), or the default. So the same script can be tuned per object without changing code.

docs.title: Reaching things
docs.text:
Inside a behaviour:

You write You get game_object, transform, name this object, its transform, its name character, rigidbody, vehicle this object's physics body of that kind, or nil find("Hero"), find_all(:coin) an object by name, all objects with a tag get_component(Health) another behaviour on the same object other.get_component(Player) a behaviour on another object destroy or destroy(other) removes an object from the game

docs.title: Setting a level up in Ruby
docs.text:
Instead of attaching scripts object by object, a level can have a scene script: scripts/main_scene.rb for scene.glb, scripts/level2_scene.rb for scenes/level2.glb. Its setup runs when the level loads, before any behaviour starts.

class MainScene < SceneScript
  ENEMY_SPEEDS = { "Slime" => 1.5, "Bat" => 4.0 }

  def setup
    find!("Player").add_component(Player, speed: 6.0)
    ENEMY_SPEEDS.each { |name, speed| find!(name).add_component(Patrol, speed: speed) }
    find_all("coin").each { |coin| coin.add_component(Coin) }
  end
end

find! is find that stops with a clear error when the object is missing. With a scene script the level file says what is there and where, and Ruby says what it does.

docs.title: When a script fails
docs.text: An error in a behaviour does not stop the game. That behaviour is switched off, and the Console shows the error with the file and line. Fix it, press Play again.

docs.title: Gameplay recipes
docs.text: Short answers to "how do I...". Each snippet goes inside a behaviour.

docs.title: Read the keyboard
docs.text:
Input.axis(:horizontal)        # -1..1: A/D or left/right arrows
Input.axis(:vertical)          # -1..1: S/W or down/up arrows
Input.action_pressed?(:jump)   # true on the frame Space goes down
Input.action?(:run)            # true while Left Shift is held
Input.down?(:e)                # any key: held
Input.pressed?(:e)             # any key: went down this frame

Built-in actions: :jump (Space), :fire (Left Ctrl or Enter), :run (Left Shift).

docs.title: Move a character
docs.text:
Give the object a character body: set Body in the Inspector's Physics card (objects made in the editor already have one), or use Add Component > Physics body on an object without physics. A character walks on floors, climbs slopes and is stopped by walls.

def update(_dt)
  direction = Vector3.new(Input.axis(:horizontal), 0, -Input.axis(:vertical)).normalized
  character.move(direction * 6.0)                                    # meters per second
  character.jump(9.0) if Input.action_pressed?(:jump) && character.grounded?
end

docs.title: Push things around
docs.text:
A dynamic body falls, rolls and gets pushed. From a script:

rigidbody.add_impulse(Vector3.up * 5.0)
rigidbody.velocity = Vector3.new(0, 0, -10)

A kinematic body is moved by your script (set transform.position) and carries what stands on it: platforms, lifts, doors.

docs.title: Drive a car
docs.text:
Give the chassis a vehicle body and mark its wheel children with wheel = true.

def fixed_update(_dt)
  vehicle.drive(throttle: Input.axis(:vertical), steering: Input.axis(:horizontal),
                handbrake: Input.down?(:space) ? 1.0 : 0.0)
end

vehicle.speed is in meters per second, negative in reverse.

docs.title: Pickups and zones
docs.text:
Tick Trigger in the object's Physics card (it stops being solid) and react when something enters:

class Coin < Behaviour
  def on_trigger_enter(other)
    return unless other.get_component(Player)

    Audio.play(:coin)
    destroy
  end
end

Only moving things (characters, dynamic and kinematic bodies) set triggers off.

docs.title: Spawn objects
docs.text:
Mark an object as a Template in the Inspector (prefab = true). It disappears from the game and becomes something to copy:

bullet = Scene.spawn("Bullet", position: transform.position, rotation: transform.rotation)
bullet.add_component(Bullet, speed: 30.0)

The copy comes with the template's physics and scripts.

docs.title: Look ahead with a ray
docs.text:
hit = Physics.raycast(transform.position, transform.forward, 20.0, game_object)
Debug.log("I see #{hit[:object].name} #{hit[:distance]} m away") if hit

The last argument is an object the ray ignores (usually the one casting it).

docs.title: Show text on screen
docs.text:
Call it every frame from update:

UI.text("Coins #{@coins}/#{@total}", x: 20, y: 40, size: 28, color: :gold)

Colors: :white, :black, :red, :green, :blue, :yellow, :gold, :orange, :gray, or [r, g, b].

docs.title: Play sounds and music
docs.text:
Files go in the game's sounds/ folder.

Audio.play(:jump)                      # sounds/jump.wav (or .ogg, .mp3, .flac)
Audio.play(:hit, volume: 0.5, pitch: 1.2)
Audio.music(:theme, loop: true)
Audio.stop_music

docs.title: Change level
docs.text:
Game.load_scene("level2")   # scenes/level2.glb; "main" is scene.glb

The switch happens at the end of the frame. Ruby global variables survive it, which is the simple way to carry a score or lives from one level to the next.

docs.title: Keep score across objects
docs.text:
Put a manager behaviour on one object and let the others find it:

class GameManager < Behaviour
  attr_reader :coins

  def self.instance = Scene.find("GameManager")&.get_component(GameManager)

  def start = @coins = 0
  def collect_coin = @coins += 1
end

# anywhere else
GameManager.instance.collect_coin

docs.title: Time
docs.text: Time.elapsed is seconds since the game started, Time.delta the length of the last frame.
